alt: A standard line and three comparison lines labelled A, B and C, with B the match. Four confederates give the same wrong answer before the real participant. Results: conformity on roughly a third of critical trials, about three-quarters conformed at least once, about a quarter never did. Strength and weakness cards follow.
caption: Even on an easy task, a unanimous wrong majority produced conformity on about a third of critical trials.

alt: Three schematic panels. Group size: conformity is very low with one confederate, rises sharply with two and three, then levels off. Anonymity: writing answers privately lowered conformity compared with saying them aloud. Task difficulty: making the lines more similar raised conformity. Cards add personality and expertise as dispositional factors.
caption: Bigger majorities (up to a point), public answers and harder tasks raise conformity.

alt: A row of 30 switches from 15 to 450 volts. All 40 participants reached at least 300 volts. Below, 40 figures with 26 coloured show that 26 of 40, 65 percent, went to the maximum 450 volts, despite obvious distress.
caption: Every participant reached 300 volts; 65% went all the way to 450.

alt: An arrow leads from the autonomous state, acting on your own conscience, to the agentic state, carrying out someone else's wishes. Cards give the four social factors: agency, authority, culture and proximity. A proximity sequence shows obedience falling with the learner in the same room, with hand-on-plate, and to around a fifth with orders by telephone.
caption: In the agentic state responsibility passes upward; authority and proximity change how far people obey.

alt: Three linked stages: harsh, strict discipline and conditional love in childhood; hostility that cannot be expressed towards parents; and an adult with rigid thinking, respect for higher status and contempt for lower status. It is measured with the F-scale. Supporting evidence and a weakness follow.
caption: A harsh upbringing produces an adult who defers to authority: measured by the F-scale.

alt: The cane victim, who appeared ill, received spontaneous help on the great majority of trials; the drunk victim on about half. A balance weighs the cost of not helping (guilt, blame) against the cost of helping (effort, danger, embarrassment, disgust). Helping a drunk person seemed more costly. Strength and weakness cards follow.
caption: Bystanders weigh the cost of helping against the cost of not helping.
